sections.heading: The Delhi Sultanate — Islam's Indian state

blocks.text: The **Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)** — established after **Muhammad Ghori's** victories (Tarain 1192) and **Qutbuddin Aibak's** accession — was **Islamic rule's first enduring north-Indian state**, spanning five dynasties: **Slave/Mamluk (Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia, Balban), Khilji (Alauddin — market reforms, Deccan raids), Tughlaq (Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiments, Firoz Shah), Sayyid, Lodi (till Babur, 1526)**.

rows: **Iltutmish** (consolidator; Qutb Minar completed; iqta system); **Razia** (first woman ruler); **Balban** (theory of kingship — 'zill-i-ilahi', strong monarchy)
**Alauddin Khilji** — **market/price control**, revenue reforms, standing army, defeated Mongols; **Malik Kafur's Deccan-South raids** reached the Andhra-Tamil country
**Muhammad bin Tughlaq** — the 'ideas ahead of time' failures (capital shift to Daulatabad, token currency); **Firoz Shah** — public works, jizya, canals; the empire fragments
Decline; **Ibrahim Lodi** defeated by **Babur at Panipat (1526)** — end of the Sultanate, birth of the Mughals

sections.heading: Advent of Islam and its impact — and craft

items: **Administrative-political impact**: the **iqta system** (revenue-assignment for military service), a centralised Persianised bureaucracy, standing armies, new coinage (tanka-jital), and the **Sultanate's model** that the Mughals inherited and perfected; Persian became the language of administration.

**Socio-cultural synthesis (the balanced view)**: the encounter produced **Indo-Islamic culture** — architecture (the arch-dome-minaret + Indian craft → Qutb complex, Alai Darwaza), **Urdu/Hindavi's genesis, Sufism's spread, music (Amir Khusrau — qawwali, sitar-tabla tradition), cuisine, and the Bhakti-Sufi dialogue (HCOI-018)**; alongside conflict (temple destruction, jizya) there was profound cultural fusion — present BOTH honestly, avoiding one-sided narratives.
**Economic impact**: urbanisation, trade expansion (Delhi a world city — Ibn Battuta), new crafts-technology (paper, spinning wheel, water-lifting devices), and market integration.

**AP/Deccan impact (the crucial state link)**: **Malik Kafur's raids (1309-11) and later Tughlaq expansion reached the Andhra-Deccan** — shattering the Kakatiyas (Warangal fell 1323) and Yadavas; the resulting political vacuum and Hindu-resistance response produced **Vijayanagara (1336) and the Bahmani Sultanate (1347)** — the Sultanate's southern impact DIRECTLY created the Deccan-AP medieval order (HCOI-020).

sections.heading: Bhakti and Sufi movements — devotion as reform

blocks.text: The medieval **Bhakti (Hindu devotional) and Sufi (Islamic mystical)** movements shared a revolutionary message: **direct, loving devotion to God over ritual-and-priesthood, equality before the divine, and vernacular expression** — a spiritual democratisation reacting to caste rigidity, ritualism and orthodoxy, and (in the Sultanate era) fostering Hindu-Muslim dialogue.

rows: **Alvars (Vaishnava) & Nayanars (Shaiva)** of Tamil country (6th-9th c.); Shankara (Advaita), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), Madhva — the philosophical-devotional foundation
**Kabir** (Hindu-Muslim synthesis, against ritual-caste), **Guru Nanak** (founded Sikhism), Dadu, Ravidas — radical social equality
**Tulsidas (Ram), Surdas (Krishna), Mirabai (Krishna), Chaitanya (Bengal Krishna-bhakti)** — emotional devotion in vernaculars
**Chishti (Moinuddin Chishti-Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya), Suhrawardi, Qadiri, Naqshbandi** silsilas; message of love (ishq), tolerance, service; the **dargah** as a shared sacred space

**Annamacharya (Annamayya — Tirumala; ~32,000 sankirtanas to Venkateswara — the founder of the Telugu padam-sankirtana tradition), Vemana (rationalist-reformist verse), Potana (Bhagavatam), Tallapaka poets, Bhakta Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna — Bhadrachalam Rama devotion)**

items: **Social impact**: Bhakti-Sufi **challenged caste and ritual hierarchy**, dignified the vernacular and the common devotee, gave women and lower castes a spiritual voice (Mira, Ravidas, Kabir), and built **Hindu-Muslim cultural bridges** (Kabir, the shared dargah culture, the syncretic saints) — a democratisation of the sacred.

**Cultural impact**: it powered the **growth of vernacular literatures** (HCOI-019) — Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Punjabi, **Telugu (Annamayya, Vemana, Potana)** — as devotional poetry became the vehicle of regional languages; and enriched **music (bhajan, kirtan, qawwali, the Carnatic-Annamayya tradition)**.

**The limits (honest note)**: Bhakti-Sufi reformed hearts more than social structures — caste largely persisted; and some later movements were absorbed back into orthodoxy — a spiritual-egalitarian impulse that softened but didn't dismantle hierarchy.

**The AP core (compulsory)**: **Annamacharya (Annamayya)** — the 15th-century Tirumala saint whose ~32,000 sankirtanas founded the **Telugu devotional-music (padam/sankirtana) tradition** — is Andhra's Bhakti crown; add **Vemana** (rationalist reform), **Potana** (Telugu Bhagavatam), and **Ramadasu (Bhadrachalam)** — Telugu Bhakti's galaxy.

sections.heading: Vernacular languages, scripts, literature and fine arts

blocks.text: The medieval period saw **regional (vernacular) languages mature into literary vehicles** — displacing Sanskrit's monopoly as **Bhakti poetry, court patronage, and administrative need** drove them; the **Apabhramsha-to-modern-language transition** produced Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, and the Dravidian quartet (Tamil, **Telugu**, Kannada, Malayalam) as full literary languages, each with its script (mostly Brahmi-derived).

rows: **Nannaya (Adikavi, 11th c.) → Tikkana → Errana (the Kavitraya's Mahabharatam); Srinatha ('Kavisarvabhaumudu'); the Vijayanagara golden age — Krishnadevaraya's Amuktamalyada & the Ashtadiggajas (Peddana, etc. — 'Prabandha' age); Potana's Bhagavatam; Vemana; Annamayya**
Bhakti poets — Kabir, Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas), Surdas; Amir Khusrau's Hindavi
Dnyaneshwar (Dnyaneshwari), Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram — the Varkari Bhakti
Kamban's Ramayana (Tamil); the Kannada three gems & Vachana poets (Basava); early Malayalam

sections.heading: Fine arts and the Telugu golden age — and craft

items: **The vernacular revolution's significance**: it **democratised literature and knowledge** (beyond the Sanskrit-knowing elite), forged **regional cultural identities** (the roots of India's linguistic states), and was inseparable from **Bhakti** (devotion needed the people's tongue) — a civilisational shift from a single classical language to a plural literary landscape.

**Fine arts**: the era saw **Indo-Islamic architecture** (arch-dome + Indian craft), **miniature painting** (later Mughal-Rajput-Deccani schools), **classical music's bifurcation into Hindustani and Carnatic** (Purandaradasa the 'father of Carnatic music'; **Annamayya's Telugu sankirtanas** feeding Carnatic), and dance (the temple-Bhakti nexus — Kuchipudi's roots in the Telugu country).

**The Telugu golden age (the crucial AP point)**: Telugu literature peaked under **Vijayanagara's Krishnadevaraya (early 16th c.)** — himself a poet (**Amuktamalyada**) — whose court hosted the **Ashtadiggajas (eight poet-elephants, led by Allasani Peddana — 'Andhrakavita Pitamaha')**, the **Prabandha (ornate narrative-poem) age**; this is Telugu literature's summit and Andhra's cultural pride.
**Craft**: the language-flowering table (Telugu first) + the vernacular-democratisation significance + the fine-arts (music-Carnatic) + the Telugu golden age (Krishnadevaraya-Ashtadiggajas).

sections.heading: The Deccan kingdoms — Kakatiyas, Vijayanagara, Bahmanis, Qutb Shahis

blocks.text: This theme is **the heart of medieval AP** — the four great Deccan powers that ruled the Telugu country between the Sultanate raids and the Mughals. Study each as a **socio-cultural** entity (the syllabus's emphasis).

rows: The first great **Telugu-identity kingdom**; **Ganapatideva, Rudramadevi (a rare woman ruler — Marco Polo praised her), Prataparudra**; **Ramappa Temple (UNESCO 2021), Warangal Fort, Thousand-Pillar Temple**; tank-irrigation (the Kakatiya tanks), inclusive nayaka-military system across castes; fell to the Tughlaqs (1323)

Founded by **Harihara & Bukka (Sangama dynasty)** as a **Hindu bulwark**; peak under **Krishnadevaraya (Tuluva, early 16th c.)** — Telugu golden age (Ashtadiggajas), temple-building (Vitthala, Virupaksha; the musical pillars, stone chariot), Roman-Persian trade, the mahanavami festival; defeated at **Talikota (1565)** by the Deccan Sultanates' alliance

The first independent **Deccan Muslim state**; **Mahmud Gawan** (great vizier — administrative reforms, the Bidar madrasa); Indo-Persian (Deccani) culture, architecture (Gol Gumbaz-lineage), Persian-Deccani Urdu; split into **five Deccan Sultanates**

The **Golconda Sultanate** — the Telugu-region Deccan Sultanate; **founded Hyderabad (Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah — Charminar, 1591)**; **Deccani-Urdu & Telugu patronage** (a rare Persianate court patronising Telugu), diamond trade (Golconda), Indo-Islamic architecture; annexed by Aurangzeb (1687)

items: **The AP significance (this is THE medieval-AP theme)**: these four kingdoms gave the Telugu country its **political identity (Kakatiyas), cultural golden age (Vijayanagara), Indo-Islamic Deccani culture (Bahmanis-Qutb Shahis), and the city of Hyderabad** — the entire medieval foundation of Andhra-Telangana; know each kingdom's socio-cultural contribution cold.

**The Hindu-Muslim Deccan interplay**: Vijayanagara (Hindu) vs the Deccan Sultanates (Muslim) were rivals AND cultural exchangers — Vijayanagara employed Muslim cavalry, the Sultanates patronised Telugu; the **Deccani culture** was itself a synthesis; Talikota (1565) was a Sultanate ALLIANCE against Vijayanagara — the political-cultural picture is nuanced, not a simple binary.

**Distinctive achievements**: **Kakatiya tank-irrigation and the Ramappa Temple; Vijayanagara's Hampi and Telugu Prabandha; the Bahmani administrative-cultural apex under Gawan; the Qutb Shahi founding of Hyderabad-Charminar and Golconda's diamonds** — the era's monuments and institutions.
**Craft**: the four-kingdom socio-cultural table (the answer's core) + the Deccan Hindu-Muslim synthesis + each kingdom's signature contribution — this is AP's medieval crown.
